newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage saga seems to enter final phase.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage saga seems to enter final phase.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis appeared to draw into its final phase late on Monday after Prime Minster Alberto Pandolfi predicted a bloodless solution and the government negotiator paid a surprise visit to the siege site.

Education Minister Domingo Palermo drove up to the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Monday evening after a day of mounting speculation that the government and Marxist hostage takers were approaching a compromise to break 13 days of stalemate.

Since the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels seized the residence in a spectacular raid on Dec. 17, both the guerrillas and the government have gradually softened conditions for the release of VIP hostages.

The guerrillas have freed more than 420 hostages since they took over the building, but 83 still remained captive, including three ambassadors, dozens of Japanese businessmen and most of the top brass of Peru's police and intelligence forces.
"We are sure that the continuing sound handling of the situation will allow a solution that protects the physical well-being and lives of all of the hostages," Pandolfi said in a speech.
"The government is working permanently with prudence and dedication for the prompt release" of the hostages, he added.

His cabinet colleague Palermo, the man picked by President Alberto Fujimori to negotiate with the guerrillas, drove up to the residence a few hours later, prompting predictions that the remaining hostages were about to walk to freedom.
Palermo's arrival was preceded by a burst of activity from around 7 p.m. EST (2300 GMT) at the residence, in Lima's fashionable San Isidro district.

A bus similar to those that have taken away freed hostages on previous days drove up to the residence and police allowed journalists to move closer to the compound. Red Cross representative Michael Minning appeared at the home -- and left again. So did Palermo.

Local television news speculated that there had been a last-minute hitch in working out the logistics of a solution providing for the release of the hostages and safe passage for the MRTA after surrendering their arms.
Fujimori, in his only public reaction to the incident, pledged in a blunt, two-minute speech nine days ago not to use force if the hostage takers laid down their arms.
Sources close to Fujimori said on Monday the president had held frequent meetings with the government's security adviser, Valdimiro Montesinos, since the Dec. 17 raid.
A shadowy and controversial figure, Montesinos has played a key role in cracking down on Peru's left-wing guerrillas since Fujimori won elections in 1990.

Pandolfi's confident statement on ending the crisis reflected a new mood of hope since the first face-to-face meeting on Saturday between the guerrillas and Palermo, which resulted in the release of 20 more hostages.

In what diplomats saw as an attempt by the guerrillas to portray themselves as respectable negotiating partners, the international spokesman of the MRTA on Monday condemned a "solidarity" bomb attack on the Peruvian Embassy in Athens.
A group identifying itself as the Guerrilla Fighting Group claimed credit for the attack, in which one woman was injured.
"We reject this sort of display of solidarity because it does not contribute to the solution of a crisis," Isaac Velazco told Reuters in an interview from Hamburg, Germany.

As the New Year approached, police and civil leaders called on Peruvians to tone down celebrations in sympathy with the hostages and to refrain from using fireworks -- particularly around the residence -- so as not to alarm the rebels.

Despite hopes for a peaceful resolution to the crisis, Peruvian anti-terrorism police sources said crack troops had completed their preparations for a possible assault on the residence if needed as a last resort.

And yet in another sign the crisis is easing, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Tuesday he would go ahead with a five-nation Asian tour next week despite the hostage crisis. Earlier this week foreign ministry officials said he may cancel the trip because of the siege.
